name: Jangkang
confidence_why: No published description of Jangkang stress exists: Smith 2019, Smith 2017 and Rensch et al. 2012 say only that the Land Dayak languages as a group stress the final syllable, so final stress for Jangkang is an inference from its family rather than a documented fact.

(Author-site copy of the University of Hawai'i Press typeset article, copyright line p. 111, PDF title '06_Smith_Article 110.142'; saved as, 33 pp.) Corroborating family-level statements: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. Smith 2017 printed p. 185 = physical p. 215, sec. 2.8.2 (text layer). Rensch et al. 2012 p. 293, sec. 6.2.4 (text layer).
catalog_quote: From a historical point of view, the existence of a full/reduced vowel distinction in the penultimate syllable is unexpected for two reasons: 1) the modern Land Dayak languages are stress-final, a pattern which is likely reconstructable to the proto-language. It is typologically unexpected for unstressed vowels to have a greater number of distinctions than stressed vowels. [fn. 2, p. 112:] ... Southern Land Dayak includes Golik, Kembayan, Jangkang, Ribun, and Sanggau, among others. [Smith 2017 p. 185, sec. 2.8.2:] Most importantly, stress in many of the languages of West Kalimantan is consistently word-final, a feature of most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area. [Rensch et al. 2012 p. 293, sec. 6.2.4:] ... an accentual difference is not evident in the contemporary Land Dayak languages. They consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word in all modern Land Dayak languages, a group that includes Jangkang (Southern Land Dayak). Corroborated at family level by Smith 2017 p. 185 ('stress in many of the languages of West Kalimantan is consistently word-final, a feature of most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area') and Rensch et al. 2012 p. 293 ('[the contemporary Land Dayak languages] consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position'). No source states the rule for Jangkang by name.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Jangkang. Rensch et al. 2012 p. 293 add that final accent is 'especially evident in utterance-final position'; Smith 2017 p. 152 and Smith 2019 discuss reduced/merged penultimate vowels (Jangkang penult *a/*ə > o) consistent with unstressed penults.
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level generalization (Land Dayak / Southern Land Dayak), not a Jangkang-specific description; word-level stress; Rensch et al. restrict the Bidayuh statement to citation forms and stems. Smith's Land Dayak data include his own Jangkang wordlist (Semirau village), so the generalization presumably covers his Jangkang data, but no Jangkang phonology has been published.
new_statements.identity_note: Jangkang (Glottolog jang1257, ISO djo; ISO name 'Djongkang' until 2008). Speakers call the language Bekidoh/Bokidoh (Untan articles). Ethnologue/id.wikipedia dialects: Jangkang proper and Pompang. The quoted statements are about Land Dayak as a whole (Smith 2019, Rensch et al. 2012) or the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas area (Smith 2017); Jangkang is placed in Southern Land Dayak with Ribun (ribu1245), Golik, Sanggau (sang1339) and Kembayan (kemb1250). Smith's Land Dayak data include his own Jangkang wordlist from Semirau village.

new_statements.quote: Other than a few unexplained full vowels that may be very early borrowings, all other reflexes of PMP penultimate vowels are reduced. The regular outcome is therefore a reduced penultimate vowel, no doubt brought about by the strong word-final stress system of LD languages.

new_statements.relation_note: Same family-level final-stress claim as the existing statement (Smith 2019, OL 58: 111 'the modern Land Dayak languages are stress-final') and the other family-level sources already logged for this glottocode (Smith 2017 p. 185; Rensch et al. 2012 p. 293). Adds nothing Jangkang-specific; the paper's subject is Mali, Beaye and Ba'aje (Benyadu-Bekati' subgroup), with Jangkang cited only as comparative data. The catalog record itself has an empty rule; this work supports fixed: final syllable only at the Land Dayak family level.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A passing family-level remark: Land Dayak languages as a group have strong word-final stress, invoked to explain the reduction of penultimate vowels. The paper has no phonology/prosody section and makes no statement about Jangkang specifically; Jangkang appears only as a Southern Land Dayak witness for high-vowel monophthongization (Table 6, p. 7: Jangkang oti 'liver' < PLD *atay).
new_statements.identity_note: The one listed work (Smith & Sommerlot 2023, JSEALS 16.2) is about Mali, Beaye and Ba'aje (Benyadu-Bekati' subgroup of Land Dayak), not Jangkang; Jangkang (Southern Land Dayak, Smith's own fieldwork from Semirau, Sanggau Regency) is cited only as comparative data in Table 6. Its stress remark is generic to 'LD languages'.
